doc.title: Paul Smith interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 14, 1999

title: Playing piano with a shoe on his hand
summary: On a triplet date the producer wanted only a ching-ching sound, so he played with a shoe, and he told the contractor not to call him for such dates.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: I have to ask the obvious question to me, is what key was that piece in if you were playing with your shoe on?

It doesn’t make any difference. It’s just the sound, ching-ching-ching. I didn’t make any chord changes. The shoe covered part — it was mostly on the black keys, but the lower part was on the white. So you have white and black both [scats]. But all he could hear was ching-ching-ching-ching— and that’s the sound he wanted. It didn’t make any difference what notes they were, playing a G chord or a D chord or anything like that, just ching-ching-ching that’s it.
That six-eight feel was kind of a — was it because it was a good dance feel? Is that why that became a thing?

I don’t really know. I mean I went up to him after the date and told him not to call me on those kind of dates anymore. Because I had to go right from there over and play something, and I mean I’d been playing with a shoe on my hand or [scats] and then go over and have to play something at NBC for some singer, and you’d come in like this. So I said don’t call me on those triplet date. You’ve got a musical date I’ll be happy to do it. I mean it cost me a lot of money but I’d rather come home happy than irritated.
